newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait to inject $4.95 bln in state housing bank.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait to inject $4.95 bln in state housing bank.

text.p: Kuwait's parliament authorised the government to inject 1.5 billion dinars ($4.95 billion) into the capital of a state housing loans arm.
The government bill would increase to 2.5 billion dinars the capital of the Savings and Credit Bank using funds from the state's general reserves account of seven billion dinars.
The bill, which requires the endorsement of the Emir Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah before its enactment, won a unaninous approval by 41 attending members of the 62-seat chamber.
The finance minister would decide whether the amount should be made in one or several instalments, the bill says.

MPs have often complained that Kuwaitis had to wait for years to obtain a loan from the bank, which is obliged by law to provide married Kuwaiti men with interest-free housing loans of 70,000 dinars each to be settled over an average of 70 years.

The oil-rich Gulf state, under a cradle-to-grave welfare system, provides its 720,000 nationals with free health and education services and heavily susbidises public utilities. Kuwaitis are not required to pay taxes.

"The required increase of 1,500 million dinars would fulfil the bank's financing needs until the year 2000, after which the bank faces a financing problem once more," said parliament's financial commitee of the bill.
The increase represented more than a fifth of national wealth as measured by Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
Some economists say the state cannot afford to provide such benefits to its nationals for over a decade.
The year after Iraqi troops were forced out of Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War, the state bought the banks credit portfolio of 924 million dinars and wrote off all nationals' housing loans.
The state injected 755 million dinars since the 1992 measure into the bank to enable it to continue its operations.

Kuwait projects a 1.17 billion dinars deficit in the 1997/98 (July-June) proposed budget and 1.21 billion for the current fiscal year but economists and officials say higher world oil prices would cut the shortfall.
